summary: Many Internet of Things deployments use small devices that sense or control things such as in home automation or industrial systems. This proposed standard profiles TLS and DTLS for such devices, describing which features and options they should use to get secure communication with limited resources. It also covers how these profiles fit with protocols commonly used in IoT.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny gadgets like smart light bulbs have very little memory, but still need to keep secrets. This is a short list of which locks and keys a tiny gadget should pick so it stays safe without carrying too much.

subtitle: Which TLS and DTLS 1.2 options a small, resource-limited device should use to talk securely.

tldr.problem: Constrained Internet of Things devices often ship without communication security, and full TLS and DTLS offer far more options than such devices can afford to implement.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC profiles TLS and DTLS 1.2 by picking one mandatory ciphersuite per credential type (pre-shared key, raw public key, certificate), and by saying which extensions and features to require, recommend or avoid.
tldr.outcome: Implementers get a short list of settings that prevents eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery without changing TLS or DTLS or adding any extension. It remains a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Recommended initial DTLS timer
facts.value: 9 seconds, back off to no less than 60 seconds

facts.label: Server certificate chain support
facts.value: at least 3, not counting the trust anchor

today: RFC 7925 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It targets TLS and DTLS 1.2, and the text itself says TLS 1.3 was then under development and not expected to just work with this profile.

sections.title: A Profile of TLS and DTLS for Constrained Devices
sections.content:
An engineer building an IoT device must decide which security services to use. Authentication of both endpoints, integrity and confidentiality are often needed, and TLS and DTLS are popular with many application protocols. The main goal here is to protect Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) messages using DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347), but the guidance is not limited to CoAP or DTLS.

A profile means the available configuration options and extensions are used in the way that best suits the IoT environment. The document does not alter TLS or DTLS and introduces no new extension. Its target audience is the embedded developer configuring a TLS or DTLS stack.

It covers version 1.2 of both protocols (RFC 5246 for TLS). The text notes that TLS 1.3 was then under development and that this profile is not expected to just work with it.
sections.plainLanguage: A full toolbox has hundreds of tools, but a tiny gadget can only carry a few. This RFC says which few tools to pack.

sections.title: Constrained Clients and Constrained Servers
sections.content:
The RFC describes two communication architectures. In the first, a constrained client talks to one or more servers. It must know each server's address and which credentials to use, supplied for example in a firmware package or by a configuration protocol. In the second, constrained servers wait for ordinary clients, usually with help from an authentication and authorization server that holds access policies and distributes keying material.

Worked examples show what this looks like. EAP-TLS for network access authentication lets a device reuse most of its TLS code, saving flash memory, though the credentials for network access and for application security are very likely different. In a CoAP example, a sensor acts as DTLS client to a resource directory, registers its resources, and later answers a relayed GET over the already established DTLS record layer. In a local example, a thermostat discovers a temperature sensor and a fan using the multicast address FF02::FD.

For constrained servers the RFC names three challenges: discovery and reachability, authentication (credential provisioning, by pairing or by a trusted third party), and authorization. It points to the IETF ACE work for finer-grained, more dynamic access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the tiny gadget knocks on a big server's door, and sometimes the gadget is the one waiting inside. Either way, both sides need to know the secret knock before the door opens.

sections.title: Ciphersuites and Key Sizes
sections.content:
A ciphersuite bundles the authentication and key exchange algorithm, the cipher and key length, the mode of operation, the hash algorithms, and notes such as authentication tag length. TLS 1.2 added Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) suites, which encrypt and authenticate at once. AES-CCM is the example mode. The suite name ending in _8 uses an 8-octet authentication tag, while regular CCM suites have 16-octet tags. The shorter tag saves bandwidth but raises the chance that an attacker can present a forged message that passes verification.

Implementations conformant to this profile MUST use AEAD ciphers. The truncated MAC extension (RFC 6066) and encrypt-then-MAC (RFC 7366) do not apply and MUST NOT be used.

On key lengths, the RFC reproduces a table of comparable sizes from RFC 4492. It notes that DH keys of at least 2048 bits correspond to a 112-bit symmetric key and a 233-bit ECC key. It chooses 112-bit keys conservatively because IoT devices may live 10 or more years. It also advises headroom for upgrading algorithms and mentions ChaCha20 with Poly1305 as a possible future choice. It does not recommend or mandate a specific ECC curve.

Perfect forward secrecy (PFS) protects past traffic if a long-term secret is later compromised. The PSK suite does not offer it, because no Diffie-Hellman exchange is used, while the public-key suites do. Implementations SHOULD NOT reuse ephemeral DH keys across exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: A ciphersuite is a recipe card for the lock and key. The RFC picks short recipes that a small gadget can cook quickly, even if they are a little less roomy than the full-size ones.

sections.title: Pre-Shared Keys and Raw Public Keys
sections.content:
The RFC defines mandatory-to-implement behaviour per credential type. It first requires that a different key pair be provisioned for each device, preferably generated on the device itself, and that credentials be created with enough entropy. Deriving a shared secret from a password or device identifiers is not secure.

Pre-shared key (PSK) is computationally efficient and bandwidth conserving. The client names its key by a PSK identity in the ClientKeyExchange message. PSK identities SHOULD NOT have a structured format, and the server MUST compare them byte by byte. Implementations MAY use identities up to 128 octets and keys up to 64 octets, and shorter identities are RECOMMENDED. A compliant device MUST implement TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8.

Raw public keys (RFC 7250) give a first step into public key cryptography without certificates or a PKI. The key is carried in the Certificate message, with the client_certificate_type and server_certificate_type extensions to indicate support. A compliant device MUST implement TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8, which uses ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman and ECDSA.

In DTLS, the server may send a HelloVerifyRequest cookie to resist flooding. A server need not do this every time, but the client must be ready to respond.
sections.plainLanguage: A pre-shared key is a secret password both sides already know. A raw public key is more like a personal lock whose matching key you were handed ahead of time, with no big paperwork.

sections.title: Certificates in the Profile
sections.content:
For certificate-based authentication, the same ciphersuite TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 is mandatory. Support for the cached_info extension (RFC 7924) is REQUIRED, so a client can avoid receiving the same certificate chain on every full handshake. The recommended curve is secp256r1 with uncompressed points.

Server certificates must put a fully qualified DNS name in the subjectAltName, not in the Common Name. They MUST NOT contain wildcard names or multiple names. Client certificates must carry an EUI-64 identifier. Devices MUST support a server certificate chain of at least 3, not counting the trust anchor, and MAY reject longer ones.

Certificates are X.509 v3 and signed with ECDSA using SHA-256 or stronger, including CA certificates. Limiting algorithms like this reduces the flash memory needed for code. Revocation does not use OCSP or CRLs. The profile relies on a software update mechanism to provision information about revoked certificates, and further study is needed on OCSP stapling.

Clients MUST implement client certificate URLs where certificates are used and the server is not constrained, but this is NOT RECOMMENDED for constrained servers. The trusted CA indication is NOT RECOMMENDED for fixed, preconfigured server sets and RECOMMENDED for dynamically discovered servers.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate is an ID card signed by someone trusted. The RFC says which kind of ID card to accept, so a gadget does not need a drawer full of different card readers.

sections.title: Extensions and Features to Use or Avoid
sections.content:
The RFC goes through the optional parts of TLS and DTLS and states a position on each:

  • Signature algorithms: the client MUST send the extension to select SHA-256. Without it, RFC 5246 defaults to SHA-1 with ECDSA. It does not apply to the PSK suite.
  • Session resumption: constrained clients MUST implement it, as it cuts messages, computation and bandwidth. If the server is constrained but not the client, the client MUST implement ticket-based RFC 5077.
  • Compression: NOT RECOMMENDED, because of attacks and added code size.
  • Server Name Indication: REQUIRED unless the client is known not to talk to servers in a hosting environment.
  • Maximum fragment length: clients MUST support it. It lowers the record size from 2^14 bytes to 2^9 bytes, saving RAM.
  • Session hash (RFC 7627): clients SHOULD implement it, to prevent the triple handshake attack.
  • False Start: RECOMMENDED when the client sends application data first, and the public-key suites meet its conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Some extra features are like optional pockets on a backpack. The RFC says which pockets a small gadget must have, which are nice to have, and which to leave off to keep the bag light.

sections.title: Keep-Alive, Timeouts and Randomness
sections.content:
Keep-alive matters because firewalls and NATs drop state, and UDP timeouts are typically much shorter than TCP ones. For client-initiated one-shot or regular uploads, a keep-alive is of no use. For server-initiated messages the heartbeat extension (RFC 6520) is RECOMMENDED.

Timeouts need care on low-bandwidth links with small frames, such as 127 bytes for IEEE 802.15.4. RFC 6347 suggests an initial retransmission timer of 1 second, doubling up to no less than 60 seconds. This RFC instead RECOMMENDEDs an initial value of 9 seconds with exponential back off up to no less than 60 seconds. The worst-case wait is the same 63 seconds but with 2 retransmissions instead of 5. Sleepy nodes may pick a lower value but must keep network stability in mind.

Random numbers are a risk because IoT devices lack the entropy sources of PCs, which can lead to the same keys being generated again and again. Devices must offer ways to generate quality random numbers, and receivers should treat gmt_unix_time in the Hello random value as an opaque string, since many IoT devices lack an accurate clock.

Appendices add details for DTLS over SMS (a path MTU of 133 bytes with WDP multiplexing, otherwise 140), the 29-byte per-packet overhead of AES-128-CCM-8 in DTLS, and advice on avoiding overlapping handshake fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: If you shout and nobody answers, wait a good while before shouting again, so you do not make a noisy room even noisier. And a gadget needs a truly random dice roll to make secrets, not the same roll every time.

sections.title: Attacks, Errors and Privacy
sections.content:
Renegotiation must be disabled. Clients MUST answer server-initiated renegotiation with a no_renegotiation alert and MUST NOT start it. Downgrade is blocked by requiring version 1.2 or higher: clients MUST NOT offer a lower version or retry with one, and servers MUST send a fatal protocol_version alert if 1.2 or higher cannot be negotiated.

Error handling uses TLS alerts. Fatal alerts end the connection, and warnings may be ignored by devices that cannot log. Alerts marked RESERVED MUST NOT be used, and certificate-related alerts MUST NOT be used with PSK or raw public keys. A server MUST return decrypt_error instead of unknown_psk_identity.

Privacy: an on-path observer can see identifiers in the handshake such as the PSK identity, and resumed sessions can be correlated. The profile makes no extra effort against traffic analysis, and the IP header is not protected. Mutual authentication lets a server collect data about the device over a long time.

The security section itself stresses designing a software update mechanism into every IoT system, to fix vulnerabilities and change trust anchors and keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC locks a few doors that a sneaky visitor could use, like forcing a gadget to use an old weak lock. It also admits that people watching the street can still see that a gadget is talking.
